claim: HSV-1 proteins pUL7 and pUL51 form a complex required for efficient virus envelopment.
source: Herpes simplex virus (HSV)−1 proteins pUL7 and pUL51 form a complex required for efficient virus envelopment.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by references to prior work (Albecka et al., 2017; Roller and Fetters, 2015) in the introduction.

claim: The interaction between homologues of pUL7 and pUL51 is conserved across human herpesviruses.
source: We show that interaction between homologues of pUL7 and pUL51 is conserved across human herpesviruses, as is their association with trans-Golgi membranes.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by co-precipitation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The association of pUL7 and pUL51 homologues with trans-Golgi membranes is conserved across human herpesviruses.
source: We show that interaction between homologues of pUL7 and pUL51 is conserved across human herpesviruses, as is their association with trans-Golgi membranes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 4.

claim: The HSV-1 pUL7:pUL51 complex forms a 1:2 complex in solution.
source: Multi-angle light scattering (MALS) analysis showed the complex to elute from size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) as two peaks with molecular masses of 79.0 ± 1.8 kDa and 165.5 ± 1.1 kDa (Figure 1A), consistent with pUL7 and pUL51 forming a 1:2 heterotrimer in solution (calculated mass from amino acid sequence 84.5 kDa) that dimerizes at higher concentrations to form a 2:4 heterohexamer (calculated mass 169 kDa).
evidence: SEC-MALS data in Figure 1A shows molecular masses consistent with 1:2 stoichiometry.

claim: The HSV-1 pUL7:pUL51 complex can form higher-order oligomers (2:4 heterohexamers) at higher concentrations.
source: Multi-angle light scattering (MALS) analysis showed the complex to elute from size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) as two peaks with molecular masses of 79.0 ± 1.8 kDa and 165.5 ± 1.1 kDa (Figure 1A), consistent with pUL7 and pUL51 forming a 1:2 heterotrimer in solution (calculated mass from amino acid sequence 84.5 kDa) that dimerizes at higher concentrations to form a 2:4 heterohexamer (calculated mass 169 kDa).
evidence: SEC-MALS data in Figure 1A shows two peaks with masses consistent with 1:2 and 2:4 stoichiometries.

claim: The crystal structure of the core pUL7:pUL51 heterodimer was solved.
source: we solved the crystal structure of the core pUL7:pUL51 heterodimer.
evidence: The structure was solved by X-ray crystallography as described in the methods and shown in Figure 2.

claim: pUL7 adopts a previously-unseen compact fold.
source: While pUL7 adopts a previously-unseen compact fold, the helix-turn-helix conformation of pUL51 resembles the cellular endosomal complex required for transport (ESCRT)-III component CHMP4B and pUL51 forms ESCRT-III–like filaments, suggesting a direct role for pUL51 in promoting membrane scission during virus assembly.
evidence: Structure-based searches did not reveal similar folds, and the structure is shown in Figure 2.

claim: The helix-turn-helix conformation of pUL51 resembles the cellular ESCRT-III component CHMP4B.
source: While pUL7 adopts a previously-unseen compact fold, the helix-turn-helix conformation of pUL51 resembles the cellular endosomal complex required for transport (ESCRT)-III component CHMP4B and pUL51 forms ESCRT-III–like filaments, suggesting a direct role for pUL51 in promoting membrane scission during virus assembly.
evidence: Structural superposition shown in Figure 5A demonstrates similarity between pUL51 and CHMP4B.

claim: pUL51 forms ESCRT-III–like filaments.
source: While pUL7 adopts a previously-unseen compact fold, the helix-turn-helix conformation of pUL51 resembles the cellular endosomal complex required for transport (ESCRT)-III component CHMP4B and pUL51 forms ESCRT-III–like filaments, suggesting a direct role for pUL51 in promoting membrane scission during virus assembly.
evidence: Electron microscopy images in Figure 5E-I show pUL51(1-170) forming filaments in vitro.

claim: pUL51 has a direct role in promoting membrane scission during virus assembly.
source: While pUL7 adopts a previously-unseen compact fold, the helix-turn-helix conformation of pUL51 resembles the cellular endosomal complex required for transport (ESCRT)-III component CHMP4B and pUL51 forms ESCRT-III–like filaments, suggesting a direct role for pUL51 in promoting membrane scission during virus assembly.
evidence: This is suggested based on structural similarity to ESCRT-III and filament formation capability.

claim: Herpesviruses acquire their membrane envelopes in the cytoplasm of infected cells.
source: Herpesviruses acquire their membrane envelopes in the cytoplasm of infected cells via a molecular mechanism that remains unclear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about herpesvirus assembly cited in the introduction (Mettenleiter et al., 2009; Owen et al., 2015).

claim: The molecular mechanism by which herpesviruses acquire their membrane envelopes remains unclear.
source: Herpesviruses acquire their membrane envelopes in the cytoplasm of infected cells via a molecular mechanism that remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: pUL7 and pUL51 co-localize with Golgi markers both during infection and when co-transfected into cells.
source: pUL7 and pUL51 form a complex that co-localizes with Golgi markers both during infection and when co-transfected into cells (Albecka et al., 2017; Roller and Fetters, 2015; Nozawa et al., 2003), palmitoylation of residue Cys9 being required for pUL51 membrane association (Nozawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited in the text.

claim: Palmitoylation of residue Cys9 is required for pUL51 membrane association.
source: pUL7 and pUL51 form a complex that co-localizes with Golgi markers both during infection and when co-transfected into cells (Albecka et al., 2017; Roller and Fetters, 2015; Nozawa et al., 2003), palmitoylation of residue Cys9 being required for pUL51 membrane association (Nozawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Nozawa et al., 2003).

claim: Deletion of pUL7, pUL51, or both proteins from HSV-1 causes a 5- to 100-fold decrease in virus replication.
source: Deletion of pUL7, pUL51, or both proteins from HSV-1 causes a 5- to 100-fold decrease in virus replication (Albecka et al., 2017; Nozawa et al., 2005; Roller et al., 2014) and cells infected with HSV-1 lacking pUL7 and pUL51 accumulate unenveloped capsids in the cytoplasm (Albecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple prior studies cited.

claim: Cells infected with HSV-1 lacking pUL7 and pUL51 accumulate unenveloped capsids in the cytoplasm.
source: Deletion of pUL7, pUL51, or both proteins from HSV-1 causes a 5- to 100-fold decrease in virus replication (Albecka et al., 2017; Nozawa et al., 2005; Roller et al., 2014) and cells infected with HSV-1 lacking pUL7 and pUL51 accumulate unenveloped capsids in the cytoplasm (Albecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Albecka et al., 2017).

claim: VZV pORF53 and pORF7 co-localize with trans-Golgi markers in infected cells.
source: pORF53 and pORF7, the pUL7 and pUL51 homologues from varicella-zoster virus (VZV), co-localize with trans-Golgi markers in infected cells (Selariu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017) and deletion of pORF7 causes a defect in cytoplasmic envelopment (Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited.

claim: Deletion of VZV pORF7 causes a defect in cytoplasmic envelopment.
source: pORF53 and pORF7, the pUL7 and pUL51 homologues from varicella-zoster virus (VZV), co-localize with trans-Golgi markers in infected cells (Selariu et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2017) and deletion of pORF7 causes a defect in cytoplasmic envelopment (Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Jiang et al., 2017).

claim: Deletion of pUL7 or pUL51 from pseudorabies virus (PrV) causes defects in virus replication and the accumulation of cytoplasmic unenveloped virions.
source: Similarly, deletion of pUL7 or pUL51 from pseudorabies virus (PrV) causes defects in virus replication and the accumulation of cytoplasmic unenveloped virions (Klupp et al., 2005; Fuchs et al., 2005), and PrV pUL51 co-localizes with Golgi membranes during infection (Klupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited.

claim: PrV pUL51 co-localizes with Golgi membranes during infection.
source: Similarly, deletion of pUL7 or pUL51 from pseudorabies virus (PrV) causes defects in virus replication and the accumulation of cytoplasmic unenveloped virions (Klupp et al., 2005; Fuchs et al., 2005), and PrV pUL51 co-localizes with Golgi membranes during infection (Klupp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Klupp et al., 2005).

claim: pUL51 homologues in β- and γ-herpesviruses lack significant sequence similarity with α-herpesvirus pUL51.
source: Homologues of pUL7 and pUL51 can be identified in β- and γ-herpesviruses, although pUL51 homologues lack significant sequence similarity with α-herpesvirus pUL51 and their homology is inferred from their conserved positions in virus genomes (Lenk et al., 1997; Campadelli-Fiume et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work cited.

claim: The homology of pUL51 across herpesvirus families is inferred from conserved positions in virus genomes.
source: Homologues of pUL7 and pUL51 can be identified in β- and γ-herpesviruses, although pUL51 homologues lack significant sequence similarity with α-herpesvirus pUL51 and their homology is inferred from their conserved positions in virus genomes (Lenk et al., 1997; Campadelli-Fiume et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work cited.

claim: HCMV pUL71 associates with the Golgi compartment when expressed in isolation and with Golgi-derived virus assembly compartments during infection.
source: The putative pUL51 homologue pUL71 from HCMV, a β-herpesvirus, associates with the Golgi compartment when expressed in isolation and with Golgi-derived virus assembly compartments during infection (Dietz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Dietz et al., 2018).

claim: Deletion of HCMV pUL71 causes defects in HCMV replication, characterized by aberrant virus assembly compartments and defects in secondary envelopment.
source: Deletion of pUL71 causes defects in HCMV replication, characterized by aberrant virus assembly compartments (Womack and Shenk, 2010) and defects in secondary envelopment (Schauflinger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior studies cited.

claim: HCMV pUL103 co-localizes with Golgi markers when expressed alone or during infection.
source: Similarly, the HCMV pUL7 homologue pUL103 co-localizes with Golgi markers when expressed alone or during infection, and deletion of pUL103 causes a loss of assembly compartments, reductions in virus assembly and defects in secondary envelopment (Ahlqvist and Mocarski, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Ahlqvist and Mocarski, 2011).

claim: Deletion of HCMV pUL103 causes a loss of assembly compartments, reductions in virus assembly and defects in secondary envelopment.
source: Similarly, the HCMV pUL7 homologue pUL103 co-localizes with Golgi markers when expressed alone or during infection, and deletion of pUL103 causes a loss of assembly compartments, reductions in virus assembly and defects in secondary envelopment (Ahlqvist and Mocarski, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Ahlqvist and Mocarski, 2011).

claim: Both the pUL7 and pUL51 homologues from murine γ-herpesvirus 68 are essential for virus replication.
source: Both the pUL7 and pUL51 homologues from murine γ-herpesvirus 68 are essential for virus replication (Song et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Song et al., 2005).

claim: EBV BSRF1 associates with Golgi membranes.
source: The putative pUL51 homologue BSRF1 from Epstein-Barr virus associates with Golgi membranes and siRNA knock-down of BSRF1 in B95-8 cells prevents virion production (Yanagi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Yanagi et al., 2019).

claim: siRNA knock-down of EBV BSRF1 in B95-8 cells prevents virion production.
source: The putative pUL51 homologue BSRF1 from Epstein-Barr virus associates with Golgi membranes and siRNA knock-down of BSRF1 in B95-8 cells prevents virion production (Yanagi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Yanagi et al., 2019).

claim: KSHV pORF42 is required for efficient virion production.
source: The KSHV homologue of pUL7, pORF42, is similarly required for efficient virion production (Butnaru and Gaglia, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Butnaru and Gaglia, 2019).

claim: EBV homologues BBRF2 and BSRF1 co-precipitate from transfected cells.
source: While a direct interaction has not been shown for the pUL7 and pUL51 homologues from β- or γ-herpesviruses, the EBV homologues BBRF2 and BSRF1 have been shown to co-precipitate from transfected cells (Yanagi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Yanagi et al., 2019).

claim: Full-length pUL51 forms large soluble aggregates when purified alone.
source: Proteins were co-expressed and co-purified because pUL51 (25.5 kDa) formed large soluble aggregates when purified alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and pUL7 (33.0 kDa) was extremely prone to aggregation upon removal of the GST purification tag when purified in the absence of pUL51.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: pUL7 is extremely prone to aggregation upon removal of the GST purification tag when purified in the absence of pUL51.
source: Proteins were co-expressed and co-purified because pUL51 (25.5 kDa) formed large soluble aggregates when purified alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and pUL7 (33.0 kDa) was extremely prone to aggregation upon removal of the GST purification tag when purified in the absence of pUL51.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from protein purification experiments.

claim: The C-terminal region of pUL51 lacks regular secondary structural elements and is disordered.
source: Prior sequence analysis (Oda et al., 2016; Nozawa et al., 2003) and our bioinformatics (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) suggested that the C-terminal region of pUL51 lacks regular secondary structural elements and is disordered.
evidence: This is predicted by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and supported by prior work.

claim: The pUL7:pUL51 complex comprises a folded core with an extended region of poorly-ordered amino acids.
source: Ab initio shape analysis was performed by fitting the 2:4 scattering curve to a dummy-atom model, or simultaneously fitting both scattering curves to a dummy-residue model, with the imposition of P2 symmetry. The models thus obtained are consistent with the pUL7:pUL51 complex comprising a folded core with an extended region of poorly-ordered amino acids (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is inferred from SAXS ab initio modeling shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: pUL51 residues 29–170 are sufficient for pUL7 binding.
source: Previous truncation analysis had shown residues 29–170 of pUL51 to be sufficient for pUL7 binding (Albecka et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Albecka et al., 2017).

claim: pUL51 residues 8–142 represent the proteolysis-resistant fragment of pUL51.
source: Mass spectrometry analysis identified a smaller protein species, evident whenever the pUL7:pUL51(1–170) was analyzed by SDS-PAGE, as pUL51 residues 8–142. On the assumption that this represented the proteolysis-resistant fragment of pUL51, pUL7 was co-expressed and co-purified with pUL51(8–142).
evidence: This is inferred from mass spectrometry identification of a degradation product.

claim: The pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex is monodisperse in solution.
source: This protein complex could be readily purified and was monodisperse in solution, SEC-MALS showing the pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex to have a mass of 61.5 ± 3.1 kDa, consistent with a 1:2 complex (calculated mass 63.1 kDa) as observed for full-length pUL7:pUL51 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC-MALS analysis in Figure 1E.

claim: The pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex has a mass of 61.5 ± 3.1 kDa, consistent with a 1:2 complex.
source: This protein complex could be readily purified and was monodisperse in solution, SEC-MALS showing the pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex to have a mass of 61.5 ± 3.1 kDa, consistent with a 1:2 complex (calculated mass 63.1 kDa) as observed for full-length pUL7:pUL51 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is measured by SEC-MALS in Figure 1E.

claim: The pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex is much more compact than the full-length complex.
source: SEC-SAXS analysis (Figure 1G) showed the pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex to be much more compact (Rg = 3.0 nm; Dmax = 11.5 nm; Figure 1K; Supplementary file 1–Table S1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SAXS analysis in Figure 1G and 1K.

claim: The pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex has a globular fold.
source: The Gaussian-like appearances of a dimensionless Kratky plot of the pUL7:pUL51(8–142) scattering data, which is centered on sRg of √3 (Figure 1L), and of the corresponding p(r) profile (Figure 1K) are consistent with the protein having a globular fold.
evidence: This is inferred from SAXS analysis shown in Figure 1K and 1L.

claim: The structure of native pUL7:pUL51(8–142) was refined to 1.83 Å resolution.
source: The structure of native pUL7:pUL51(8–142) was refined to 1.83 Å resolution with residuals R = 0.195, Rfree = 0.220 and excellent stereochemistry, 99% of residues occupying the most favored region of the Ramachandran plot (Supplementary file 1–Table S2).
evidence: This is stated as a result of X-ray crystallography structure determination.

claim: The asymmetric unit of the pUL7:pUL51(8–142) crystal structure contained four copies of pUL7 and four copies of pUL51 arranged as a hetero-octamer.
source: The asymmetric unit contained four copies of pUL7 residues 11–234 and 253–296 plus eight residues from the C-terminal purification tag (see below) and four copies of pUL51 residues 24–89 and 96–125, the remaining residues of pUL7 and pUL51(8–142) being absent from electron density and presumably disordered.
evidence: This is stated as a result of crystal structure determination.

claim: The hetero-octameric pUL7:pUL51 arrangement observed in the crystal structure is an artefact of crystallization.
source: Strikingly, the molecules of pUL7 and pUL51 in the structure were arranged as a hetero-octamer, with single β-strands from each pUL7 and pUL51 molecule in the asymmetric unit forming a central β-barrel (Figure 2A). Closer inspection revealed that the pUL7 strands in this β-barrel comprised the C-terminal amino acids encoded by the restriction site and from the human rhinovirus 3C protease recognition sequence that remained following proteolytic removal of the GST purification tag. We therefore suspected that this hetero-octameric pUL7:pUL51 arrangement was an artefact of crystallization.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the β-barrel involves cloning tag residues and is not consistent with solution data.

claim: pUL7 and pUL51 residues 41–142 assemble to form a heterodimeric 'core' complex.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that pUL7 and pUL51 residues 41–142 assemble to form a heterodimeric 'core' complex and that recruitment of the additional pUL51 molecule in the native heterotrimeric complex is mediated by the N-terminal region (residues 8–40) of pUL51.
evidence: This is inferred from SEC-MALS data showing pUL7:pUL51(41–142) forms a 1:1 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).

claim: Recruitment of the additional pUL51 molecule in the native heterotrimeric complex is mediated by the N-terminal region (residues 8–40) of pUL51.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that pUL7 and pUL51 residues 41–142 assemble to form a heterodimeric 'core' complex and that recruitment of the additional pUL51 molecule in the native heterotrimeric complex is mediated by the N-terminal region (residues 8–40) of pUL51.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that removal of residues 8–40 yields a 1:1 complex instead of 1:2.

claim: pUL7 comprises two short N-terminal α-helices followed by a compact globular fold with a mixed α-helical and β-sheet topology.
source: pUL7 comprises two short N-terminal α-helices followed by a compact globular fold with a mixed α-helical and β-sheet topology containing a central anti-parallel β-sheet and two mostly-buried α-helices that are surrounded by a β-hairpin and additional helices (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pUL7 fold does not have similarity to any other domains in the Protein Data Bank.
source: Structure-based searches of the Protein Data Bank did not reveal any other domains with a similar fold, which we will henceforth refer to as the Conserved UL7(Seven) Tegument Assembly/Release Domain (CUSTARD) fold.
evidence: This is stated based on structure-based database searches.

claim: pUL51 comprises a hydrophobic loop region followed by a helix-turn-helix.
source: pUL51 comprises a hydrophobic loop region followed by a helix-turn-helix.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 2.

claim: The interaction between pUL7 and pUL51 is extensive and largely hydrophobic in nature.
source: The interaction with pUL7 is extensive and largely hydrophobic in nature (Figure 2): The hydrophobic loop of pUL51 (residues 45–50, sequence LLPAPI) interacts with pUL7 helix α2 and with a hydrophobic pocket formed by sheets β1 and β6, helices α4 and α7 and the C-terminal tail of pUL7; hydrophobic residues of pUL51 helix α1 interact with a hydrophobic face of pUL7 helix α8; and hydrophobic residues from the C-terminal portion of pUL51 helix α2 interact with hydrophobic residues from pUL7 helices α8 and α9 (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure and shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Chemical cross-linking of pUL7:pUL51(8–142) yields species with masses corresponding to 1:1 or 1:2 pUL7:pUL51 complexes.
source: As shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, incubation of the pUL7:pUL51(8–142) complex with either disuccinimidyl sulfoxide (DSSO) or disuccinimidyl dibutyric urea (DSBU) yielded species with masses corresponding to 1:1 or 1:2 pUL7:pUL51 complexes, plus some higher-order species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS-PAGE analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Five cross-links identified between pUL7 and pUL51 were not compatible with the heterodimer crystal structure.
source: Five of these crosslinks were not compatible with the heterodimer crystal structure, suggesting that they were formed by the other molecule of pUL51 in the heterotrimer, whereas other cross-links could have been formed by either pUL51 molecule.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of cross-linking data with the crystal structure.

claim: The second copy of pUL51 in the heterotrimer binds near pUL7 helices α1, α2, α6, α7, and the loop between helices α7 and α8.
source: These models showed the second copy of pUL51 to have the same general orientation relative to pUL7, binding near pUL7 helices α1, α2, α6, α7, and the loop between helices α7 and α8 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from pseudo-atomic modeling using SAXS and cross-linking restraints shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The α-, β- and γ-herpesvirus families diverged approximately 400 million years ago.
source: The α-, β- and γ-herpesvirus families diverged approximately 400 million years ago (McGeoch and Gatherer, 2005).
evidence: This is stated based on prior work (McGeoch and Gatherer, 2005).

claim: Homologues of pUL7 from α-, β- and γ-herpesviruses can be readily identified by their conserved amino acid sequences.
source: Homologues of pUL7 from α-, β- and γ-herpesviruses can be readily identified by their conserved amino acid sequences, despite relatively low sequence identities (HCMV and KSHV homologues share 17% and 16% identity, respectively, with HSV-1 pUL7).
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: The predicted secondary structures of pUL7 homologues from representative α-, β- and γ-herpesviruses are very similar to the experimentally-determined secondary structure of HSV-1 pUL7.
source: The predicted secondary structures of pUL7 homologues from representative α-, β- and γ-herpesviruses that infect humans are very similar to the experimentally-determined secondary structure of HSV-1 pUL7, strongly suggesting that these proteins will adopt the CUSTARD fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by secondary structure predictions in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: pUL7 homologues from β- and γ-herpesviruses will adopt the CUSTARD fold.
source: The predicted secondary structures of pUL7 homologues from representative α-, β- and γ-herpesviruses that infect humans are very similar to the experimentally-determined secondary structure of HSV-1 pUL7, strongly suggesting that these proteins will adopt the CUSTARD fold (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from conservation of predicted secondary structure shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The predicted secondary structures of putative β- and γ-herpesvirus pUL51 homologues closely match the prediction for HSV-1 pUL51.
source: Similarly, the predicted secondary structures of putative β- and γ-herpesvirus pUL51 homologues closely match the prediction for HSV-1 pUL51 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) despite low sequence identity (HCMV and KSHV homologues sharing 16% and 13% identity, respectively, with HSV-1 pUL51).
evidence: This is shown by secondary structure predictions in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: mCherry-tagged pUL51 homologues from HSV-1, VZV, HCMV or KSHV can be co-precipitated with GFP-tagged pUL7 homologues from the same virus.
source: GFP-tagged pUL7 homologues from human herpesviruses HSV-1, VZV, HCMV or KSHV were co-transfected with mCherry-tagged pUL51 homologues from the same virus into human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293 T cells. In all cases, pUL51-mCherry or the relevant homologue could be readily co-precipitated with the GFP-pUL7 homologue, whereas pUL51-mCherry homologues were not efficiently co-precipitated by GFP alone (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3A.

claim: The association of pUL7 and pUL51 homologues is conserved across the herpesvirus families.
source: The association of pUL7 and pUL51 homologues is therefore conserved across the herpesvirus families.
evidence: This is concluded from co-precipitation experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HSV-1 pUL7 co-precipitates with pUL51 from HSV-1 and pORF7 from VZV, but not with pUL71 from HCMV or pORF55 from KSHV.
source: GFP-tagged pUL7 was thus co-transfected with mCherry-tagged pUL51 from HSV-1 or with mCherry-tagged homologues from VZV, HCMV or KSHV. Co-precipitation was observed for HSV-1 pUL51 and for pORF7 from VZV, an α-herpesvirus, but not for the homologues from HCMV or KSHV (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3B.

claim: The pUL7:pUL51 molecular interface is partially conserved within the α-herpesvirus family, but not across families.
source: This suggested that the pUL7:pUL51 molecular interface is partially conserved within the α-herpesvirus family, but not across families.
evidence: This is inferred from co-precipitation experiments showing cross-reactivity within but not across herpesvirus families.

claim: VZV pORF53 and pORF7 share 33% and 35% identity with HSV-1 pUL7 and pUL51, respectively.
source: VZV pORF53 and pORF7 share 33% and 35% identity with HSV-1 pUL7 and pUL51, respectively.
evidence: This is stated based on sequence analysis.

claim: Several regions of conservation in α-herpesvirus pUL7 sequences overlap with the binding footprint of pUL51 in the core heterodimeric complex.
source: Mapping the conservation of α-herpesvirus pUL7 sequences onto the HSV-1 pUL7 structure reveals several regions of conservation that overlap with the binding footprint in pUL51 in the core heterodimeric complex (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is shown by conservation mapping in Figure 3E.

claim: HSV-1 pUL51 does not co-precipitate with VZV pORF53.
source: However, capture of pUL51-mCherry did not result in co-precipitation of the VZV pUL7 homologue pORF53, nor did capture of GFP-pORF53 result in co-precipitation of HSV-1 pUL51 (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3C and D.

claim: There has been co-evolution of pUL7 and pUL51 homologues such that the interaction interfaces are distinct at a molecular level.
source: We therefore conclude that, while the pUL7:pUL51 interface is partially conserved across α-herpesviruses, there has been co-evolution of pUL7 and pUL51 homologues such that the interaction interfaces are distinct at a molecular level.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of cross-reactivity between HSV-1 and VZV proteins despite sequence conservation.

claim: True pairings of interacting residues in the pUL7:pUL51 interface showed more correlated change than 94% of randomized pairings.
source: True pairings showed more correlated change than 94% of the randomized pairings and the results were little changed when different subsets of the data, including fewer strains and more interactions, were analyzed (Supplementary file 1–Table S4).
evidence: This is stated as a result of co-evolutionary analysis.

claim: There is suggestive evidence for co-evolution of the interaction interface across the α-herpesviruses.
source: This is suggestive evidence for co-evolution of the interaction interface across the α-herpesviruses.
evidence: This is concluded from statistical analysis of correlated amino acid changes at interacting sites.

claim: HSV-1 pUL51 interacts with HSV-1 pUL14.
source: In addition to interacting with pUL7, it has previously been shown that HSV-1 pUL51 is able to interact with HSV-1 pUL14 (Oda et al., 2016) and that mutation of pUL51 amino acids Ile111, Leu119 and Tyr123 to alanine disrupts this interaction.
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Oda et al., 2016).

claim: Mutation of pUL51 amino acids Ile111, Leu119 and Tyr123 to alanine disrupts the interaction with pUL14.
source: In addition to interacting with pUL7, it has previously been shown that HSV-1 pUL51 is able to interact with HSV-1 pUL14 (Oda et al., 2016) and that mutation of pUL51 amino acids Ile111, Leu119 and Tyr123 to alanine disrupts this interaction.
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Oda et al., 2016).

claim: Residues Leu119 and Tyr123 of pUL51 are completely buried in the interface between pUL7:pUL51 in the core heterodimer structure.
source: Residues Leu119 and Tyr123 are completely buried in the interface between pUL7:pUL51 in the core heterodimer structure, interacting with residues from pUL51 helix α1 and from pUL7 helices α8 and α9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Co-precipitation of myc-pUL14 with pUL51-mCherry was not detected either in the presence or absence of GFP-pUL7.
source: To test these hypotheses, pUL51-mCherry was co-transfected into mammalian cells together with GFP-pUL7 and/or myc-pUL14 and then captured using mCherry affinity resin. While GFP-pUL7 was readily co-precipitated, we could not detect co-precipitation of myc-pUL14 with pUL51-mCherry either in the presence or absence of GFP-pUL7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The pUL51:pUL14 interaction is not direct, but is instead mediated by other herpesvirus proteins.
source: As the pUL51:pUL14 interaction was previously demonstrated using infected cells or infected-cell lysates (Oda et al., 2016) it seems likely that this interaction is not direct, but is instead mediated by other herpesvirus proteins and that it may require binding of pUL51 to pUL7.
evidence: This is inferred from the inability to detect pUL51:pUL14 interaction in transfected cells.

claim: HSV-1 pUL7:pUL51 complex co-localizes with TGN46, paxillin and zyxin.
source: As previously observed, HSV-1 pUL7:pUL51 complex co-localizes with both TGN46, a trans-Golgi marker, and with paxillin and zyxin at the cell periphery, markers of focal adhesions (Figure 4; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: VZV pORF53:pORF7, HCMV pUL103:pUL71 and KSHV pORF42:pORF55 all co-localize with TGN46 at trans-Golgi membranes.
source: VZV pORF53:pORF7, HCMV pUL103:pUL71 and KSHV pORF42:pORF55 all co-localize with TGN46 at trans-Golgi membranes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 4.

claim: VZV pORF53:pORF7, HCMV pUL103:pUL71 and KSHV pORF42:pORF55 do not co-localize with paxillin or zyxin at focal adhesions.
source: However, these homologues do not co-localize with paxillin or zyxin at focal adhesions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence microscopy in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Helices α1 and α2 of pUL51 superpose onto human CHMP4B with 1.2 Å root-mean-squared deviation across 59 Cα atoms.
source: Helices α1 and α2 of pUL51 superpose onto human CHMP4B (Martinelli et al., 2012) with 1.2 Å root-mean-squared deviation across 59 Cα atoms (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 5A.

claim: pUL51 resembles the structures of yeast and fly CHMP4B homologues Snf7 and Shrub.
source: pUL51 also resembles the structures of yeast and fly CHMP4B homologues Snf7 (Tang et al., 2015) and Shrub (McMillan et al., 2016), and pUL51 can be superposed onto either structure with 1.5 Å root-mean-squared deviation across 57 Cα atoms (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: CHMP4B and homologues are required for the efficient fusion of membrane leaflets during vesicle budding into organelle lumens, cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope closure, and budding of some enveloped viruses.
source: CHMP4B and homologues are required for the efficient fusion of membrane leaflets during vesicle budding into organelle lumens, cytokinetic abscission, nuclear envelope closure, and budding of some enveloped viruses (McCullough et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work (McCullough et al., 2018).

claim: A conserved feature of cellular ESCRT-III components like CHMP4B is their ability to form filaments that line the neck of nascent membrane buds and act in concert with VPS4 to promote membrane scission.
source: A conserved feature of cellular ESCRT-III components like CHMP4B is their ability to form filaments that line the neck of nascent membrane buds and act in concert with VPS4 to promote membrane scission (McCullough et al., 2018; Maity et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: Formation of ESCRT-III filaments is accompanied by a conformational switch from a closed, auto-inhibited form to an open, polymerization-competent form where helix α3 is continuous with helix α2.
source: Formation of such filaments is accompanied by a conformational switch from a closed, auto-inhibited form to an open, polymerization-competent form where helix α3 of the ESCRT-III core domain is continuous with helix α2 (Tang et al., 2015; McMillan et al., 2016; McCullough et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: The region of pUL51 immediately following helix α2 is predicted to be helical.
source: The region of pUL51 immediately following helix α2 is predicted to be helical (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by secondary structure predictions in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: pUL51(1-170) forms filaments in vitro.
source: Negative stain electron microscopy analysis of the pUL51(1–170) protein prepared in buffers lacking salt showed it to form filaments in vitro.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 5E-I.

claim: The form of pUL51(1-170) filaments varies with pH, concentration and incubation time on the electron microscopy grid.
source: The form of these filaments varied with pH, concentration and incubation time on the electron microscopy grid: Short proto-filaments with diameters of 20–28 nm were formed by 100 µM pUL51(1–170) at pH 8.5 in the absence of salt incubated on grids for 30 s before staining (Figure 5E–G), whereas longer 12–15 nm wide filaments were formed by 10 µM pUL51(1–170) in pH 7.5 HEPES incubated on grids for 1–2 min before staining (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy images in Figure 5E-I.

claim: pUL51(1–170) filaments resemble the filaments observed in vitro for purified Snf7 and CHMP4B.
source: These pUL51(1–170) filaments resemble the filaments observed in vitro for purified Snf7 (Henne et al., 2012) and CHMP4B (Pires et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with prior work.

claim: pUL51 shares the ability to form filaments in vitro with cellular ESCRT-III components.
source: Therefore, in addition to sharing structural similarity to cellular ESCRT-III components, pUL51 shares the ability to form filaments in vitro.
evidence: This is concluded from electron microscopy observations and comparison with ESCRT-III.

claim: The C-terminal region of ESCRT-III components promotes stabilization of the closed, auto-inhibited form.
source: As the C-terminal region of ESCRT-III components promote stabilization of the closed, auto-inhibited form (Bajorek et al., 2009; Henne et al., 2012), we used a truncated form of pUL51 spanning residues 1–170 that is predicted to be largely α-helical in nature (Figure 5D; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: pUL51(1-170) expressed in E. coli in the absence of pUL7 was insoluble.
source: When expressed in E. coli in the absence of pUL7 this protein was insoluble (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by purification from inclusion bodies shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: pUL51(1-170) could be readily purified from inclusion bodies and refolded in vitro by rapid dilution.
source: However, the protein could be readily purified from inclusion bodies and refolded in vitro by rapid dilution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by purification and refolding shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Refolded pUL51(1-170) is largely α-helical.
source: Circular dichroism spectroscopy of the refolded protein confirmed it to be largely α-helical (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by circular dichroism spectroscopy in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Refolded pUL51(1-170) was soluble at low salt concentrations (≤200 mM).
source: While the refolded protein was soluble at low salt concentrations (≤200 mM), it rapidly aggregated to form visible precipitates at higher salt concentrations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from protein purification experiments.

claim: Refolded pUL51(1-170) rapidly aggregated to form visible precipitates at salt concentrations higher than 200 mM.
source: While the refolded protein was soluble at low salt concentrations (≤200 mM), it rapidly aggregated to form visible precipitates at higher salt concentrations.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from protein purification experiments.

claim: pUL7 acts as a chaperone of pUL51, regulating its polymerization by physically inhibiting its self-association.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that polymerization of pUL51 may utilize equivalent molecular surfaces as cellular CHMP4B homologues. We propose that pUL7 acts as a chaperone of pUL51, regulating its polymerization by physically inhibiting its self-association.
evidence: This is proposed based on structural observations and comparison with ESCRT-III regulation.

claim: Polymerization of pUL51 may utilize equivalent molecular surfaces as cellular CHMP4B homologues.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest that polymerization of pUL51 may utilize equivalent molecular surfaces as cellular CHMP4B homologues.
evidence: This is inferred from structural superposition showing pUL7 occupies space that would be occupied by adjacent ESCRT-III molecules.

claim: The N-terminal region of pUL51 is palmitoylated and this modification is required for its membrane association.
source: The N-terminal region of pUL51 is palmitoylated and this modification is required for its membrane association (Nozawa et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Nozawa et al., 2003).

claim: The N-terminal myristoylation of cellular ESCRT-III component CHMP6 is required for its membrane association.
source: These properties are shared by the N-terminally myristoylated cellular ESCRT-III component CHMP6 (Yorikawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Yorikawa et al., 2005).

claim: Activity of ESCRT-III components and VPS4 are required for efficient assembly of HSV-1.
source: Activity of ESCRT-III components and VPS4, the AAA-ATPase that dissociates ESCRT-III and promotes bud scission (McCullough et al., 2018; Maity et al., 2019), are known to be required for efficient assembly of HSV-1 (Crump et al., 2007; Pawliczek and Crump, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited.

claim: ESCRT-I, ESCRT-II, Alix, HD-PTP and BROX are not required for HSV-1 assembly.
source: During cellular budding events ESCRT-III proteins are recruited to sites of membrane deformation via direct interactions with components of the ESCRT-I and ESCRT-II complexes, or with the Bro1-domain containing proteins Alix, HD-PTP or BROX (Christ et al., 2017). However, these proteins are not required for HSV-1 assembly (Pawliczek and Crump, 2009; Barnes and Wilson, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by prior work cited.

claim: pUL51 may directly promote membrane deformation and virus budding.
source: The lack of requirement for cellular initiators of ESCRT-III polymerization, combined with the ability of pUL51 to bind directly to membranes and to form filaments, suggests that pUL51 may directly promote membrane deformation and virus budding – effectively performing the roles of multiple cellular ESCRT-III components.
evidence: This is proposed based on the lack of requirement for cellular ESCRT machinery and pUL51's properties.

claim: Mutation of HCMV pUL71 results in the accumulation of HCMV particles in membrane buds with narrow necks.
source: This proposal is consistent with observations made in HCMV, where mutation of the pUL51 homologue pUL71 results in the accumulation of HCMV particles in membrane buds with narrow necks (Read et al., 2019) that are reminiscent of the stalled budding profiles observed for HIV-1 when ESCRT-III activity is perturbed (von Schwedler et al., 2003) or HSV-1 in cells expressing a dominant negative form of VPS4 (Crump et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by prior work (Read et al., 2019).

claim: pUL51 and homologues act as viral ESCRT-III components.
source: Based on the structural and functional homology between pUL51 and CHMP4B/CHMP6 we propose that pUL51 and homologues act as viral ESCRT-III components.
evidence: This is proposed based on structural similarity and functional properties.

claim: The interaction between pUL7 and pUL51 homologues regulates polymerization of pUL51 homologues in infected cells.
source: The interaction between pUL7 and pUL51 homologues is conserved across herpesviruses, and we propose that this interaction regulates polymerization of pUL51 homologues in infected cells.
evidence: This is proposed based on the conserved interaction and structural observations.

claim: Deletion of pUL51 or its homologues does not completely abolish virus replication.
source: Furthermore, as deletion of pUL51 or its homologues does not completely abolish virus replication (Albecka et al., 2017; Nozawa et al., 2005; Roller et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Klupp et al., 2005; Schauflinger et al., 2011; Yanagi et al., 2019) it is likely that herpesviruses use multiple, redundant mechanisms to ensure efficient wrapping of nascent virions.
evidence: This is stated based on prior work cited.

claim: Herpesviruses likely use multiple, redundant mechanisms to ensure efficient wrapping of nascent virions.
source: Furthermore, as deletion of pUL51 or its homologues does not completely abolish virus replication (Albecka et al., 2017; Nozawa et al., 2005; Roller et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Klupp et al., 2005; Schauflinger et al., 2011; Yanagi et al., 2019) it is likely that herpesviruses use multiple, redundant mechanisms to ensure efficient wrapping of nascent virions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that deletion of pUL51 does not completely abolish replication.

claim: pUL7 occupies the space that would be occupied by the adjacent Shrub molecule of a putative Shrub homopolymer.
source: Superposition of the pUL7:pUL51 core heterodimer onto Shrub shows that pUL7 occupies the space that would be occupied by the adjacent Shrub molecule of a putative Shrub homopolymer (Figure 5J; McMillan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The DM14-3 domain of Lgd occupies a similar space to helices α8 and α9 of pUL7.
source: Similarly, the DM14-3 domain of Lgd, which is sufficient to bind Shrub in vitro and prevent Shrub polymerization (McMillan et al., 2017), occupies a similar space to helices α8 and α9 of pUL7 (Figure 5K).
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural superposition shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Crystallographic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank under accession code 6T5A.
source: Crystallographic coordinates and structure factors have been deposited in the Protein Data Bank, www.pdb.org (accession code 6T5A), and raw diffraction images have been deposited in the University of Cambridge Apollo repository (https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.44914).
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.

claim: SAXS data, ab initio models and pseudo-atomic models have been deposited into the Small-Angle Scattering Biological Data Bank under accession codes SASDG37, SASDG47 and SASDG57.
source: SAXS data, ab initio models and pseudo-atomic models have been deposited into the Small-Angle Scattering Biological Data Bank (SASBDB) (Valentini et al., 2015) under the accession codes SASDG37 (pUL7:pUL51(8–142) heterotrimer), SASDG47 (pUL7:pUL51 heterohexamer) and SASDG57 (pUL7:pUL51 heterotrimer).
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.

claim: Mass spectrometry data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD015941.
source: Mass spectrometry data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE (Perez-Riverol et al., 2019) partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD015941.
evidence: This is stated in the data availability section.
